blocks.text: Interrupting situations with down, sit & stand

By interruptions in the sense of ‘sit’, ‘down’ and ‘stand’ we mean all purposeful actions which, with appropriate training, allow us to divert our dog from unwanted actions by calling up a calm, controllable alternative action and at the same time to put it into a kind of controllable state of calm.

They use the principle of alternative behaviour: instead of merely suppressing an unwanted behaviour – which often creates frustration – a positive, rewardable and physically relaxing behaviour is actively called up. This leaves no void, but a clear course of action that makes sense to the dog.
Interruptions are partnership-based – they invite the dog rather than forcing it.
Effect & goal 🎯
Interruptions make it possible to put the dog into a controllable state of calm.
They also serve to establish a desired attention span towards us or towards other things – they thus promote a conscious orientation towards the human.
Interruptions have a calming effect on the dog and, when applied with a sense of proportion, put it into a mood that is, depending on the situation, calmer or at least controllable.
They help to gradually reduce impulsive reactions to environmental stimuli.
The principle of alternative behaviour 🔄
Instead of merely suppressing an unwanted behaviour – which often creates frustration – a positive, rewardable behaviour is actively called up.
The dog is not “forced” but actively invited to choose a behavioural alternative that is more pleasant for everyone involved.
This leaves no void, but a clear course of action that makes sense to the dog.
How well do interruptions work? 📊
How reliably interruptions can be called up is determined exclusively by long-term, regular training in the widest variety of situations and stimulus levels.
The handler's ability to make their way of communicating understandable and predictable for the dog, according to the situation and stimulus level, is the key element of successful training.
Clear, consistent signals and calm emotional self-control on the part of the human are decisive here – dogs primarily read our body language, our voice modulation and our timing of the reward.
Interruptions are correct procedures in which accuracy, motivation and calmness are closely interwoven in training, and which demand situation-dependent empathy and perseverance from the handler.
Non-violent training principles 🕊️

They are based on modern, non-violent training principles: instead of stopping through pressure or intimidation (e.g. a loud “no” without a clear alternative), the unwanted behaviour is interrupted by a positive signal and immediately replaced by a rewarded alternative behaviour.
This strengthens the bond, reduces frustration and promotes intrinsic motivation.
Choosing the right exercise 🧩
The diversity of the different interruption exercises demands considerable skill and feeling from the handler with regard to the situation at hand.

Depending on the level of arousal, physical condition and previous training level, a relaxed “down” may lead to the desired goal in one situation – and in other situations a “sit” or even a brief “stand” may be the means of choice.

Which procedure is used in which situation is determined by a mix of experience – that is, a large number of training sessions with the dog in the most varied situations – and quick assessment of the current situation.
Decisive for a successful outcome is the appropriate choice of the suitable interruption variant – always matched to the dog's current state of arousal, physical ability and training level.
Response control & trust 🤝
Well-trained interruptions strengthen the dog's response control and frustration tolerance in the long term.
They teach it that calm, alternative behaviour is the most reliable source of positive consequences.
This creates deep trust: in difficult moments the dog learns no longer to react automatically and impulsively, but first to seek orientation from the human.
Philosophy of interruptions 💛

Viewed philosophically, interruptions embody a partnership-based attitude to the relationship: instead of dominance through suppression, cooperation is promoted through clear communication, mutual understanding and shared positive experiences.

The dog is not “forced” but actively invited to choose a behavioural alternative that is more pleasant for everyone involved. An attitude that places respect for the animal's individuality and genuine care of the relationship at the centre.
With patience, consistency and enjoyment of the shared learning process, interruptions thus develop into one of the most valuable tools for a relaxed, safe and harmonious life together with our dog.
Practical impulse: The “three-situation week”

This week, consciously choose three different everyday situations (e.g. an encounter with a dog, distraction by noises, a waiting situation) and specifically train an interruption with “sit” or “down” there. Note which variant works best in which situation – this is how you build experience and a feel for the right choice.
Interruptions are non-violent alternative actions.
They do not create a void, but clear courses of action.
Success comes from long-term training in the widest variety of situations.
The right choice depends on arousal level and training level.
They strengthen trust, frustration tolerance and bond.
Interruptions are partnership-based – they invite the dog rather than forcing it.
